html:
The Nicarao were a Nahua-speaking people of the isthmus of Rivas in southwest Nicaragua, between Lake Nicaragua and the Pacific. Their language was a form of Nawat, like that of the Pipil, and their ancestors had come south from Mexico some centuries before 1492.

They farmed maize and grew cacao, whose beans they used as money, and held markets and temples much like those of Mexico. Their neighbours and rivals were the Chorotega and the Subtiaba.

In 1523 the Spanish captain Gil González Dávila met their ruler, whom the Spanish called Nicarao, and baptised many of his people. By tradition the name of Nicaragua comes from him. Disease, war and the export of enslaved people to Panama and Peru then cut their numbers sharply.
